newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW-Australian Q2 inflation data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Australian Q2 inflation data.

text.p: Australia's consumer price index (CPI) fell 0.2 percent in the June quarter for an annual rate of 0.3 percent. Underlying inflation rose 0.3 percent in the quarter for a year-on-year rate of 1.7 percent.

Economists' forecasts had centred on a 0.1 percent fall in headline inflation for an annual rate of 0.5 percent, while underlying inflation had been expected to rise 0.4 percent for 1.7 percent annually. A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follows.
STEPHEN WHITE, ECONOMIST, GIO AUSTRALIA:

"I am not surprised that it (headline CPI) is coming down 0.2. But I am a little bit surprised about the underlying rate of inflation with information at the moment indicating it was going to be a little bit higher. But it is probably at the trough now and it will be gradually picking up over the remainder of 1997 and into 1998. It doesn't harm the case (for rate cuts). But looking 12 months ahead and looking at pretty reasonable economic conditions it is hard to find convincing reasons for another cut in interest rates at this particular point in time."
JOHN EDWARDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HONG KONG BANK OF AUSTRALIA:

"It's a splendid result and we think it meets the second of three conditions for a rate cut to be announced on Friday. The other one was the confirmed reluctance of the Federal Reserve to raise rates and the next condition is tomorrow's average weekly earnings which in our view have to display moderate overall earnings growth to permit another rate cut."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER AUSTRALIA:

"In terms of policy it's spot on market expectations, but the psychological impact of having deflation in the economy in last quarter on a headline basis is pretty powerful. The RBA will pay more attention to the underlying rate, but this is now well below the 2-3 percent target band so it just confirms we are in a very low inflation economy. We are going through a system now of ticking off indicators. The next one is wages and then the icing on the cake will be the retail trade and building approvals figures next week, which we think are going to be weak. So given a good inflation outlook and weak indicators there is a 50/50 chance that the bank will cut again."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"The inflation outcome confirms that there haven't been any inflation pressures for the last few years. We have hit a 25 year low on the underlying inflation rate, which of course is the more sensitive of the two series. So a 50 basis point interest rate cut would look almost assured, if we get a reasonably subdued wages number tomorrow. I think the Reserve Bank would ease on the back of even a 1.0 percent quarterly increase in the May quarter (wages)."
HANS KUNNEN, GROUP ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"It is encouraging for those that want a rate cut. While there is sluggish economic growth and high unemployment it has set the scene for a rate cut. I can't see how a half percent is going to do to the bigger picture of inflation. It is not the 'be all and end all' but inflation is below the (RBA's) target zone."
BILL SHIELDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"The figures are better than expected, partly because of the weakness in the economy over the past six to nine months and partly because of the continuing flow-through of a stronger A$ and lower mortgage rates. However, the figure was better than the market range and the markets have responded rather predictably. The A$ is weakened. Interest rates have strengthened a bit, but not that much bearing in mind they opened quite strongly this morning following Mr Greenspan's comments. But expectations of another official rate cut are fully built into the market now."
SEAN CALLOW, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"The figures were close to our expectations and slightly better than the market expected. It adds to the case for easings of monetary policy. Our prediction is that a move will be made after the RBA meeting in August."
DAVID BASSANESE, ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST OF AUSTRALIA LTD:

"It is a better than expected market result. The figures remove the potential hurdle to a RBA move, which we still expect to happen. The predicted RBA move on Friday is excessively exuberant. The RBA is not trigger-happy."
NIGEL STAPLEDON, ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:

"It is a pretty good number across the board. The headline number is a good number, but more importantly the underlying number is also a very impressive result. It certainly leaves the way open for another rate cut."
SHANE OLIVER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, AMP SOCIETY:

"This is a very good outcome, a very good outcome for the Reserve Bank, and I think it does pave the way for another easing. I think the Reserve Bank strategy would be to prefer to tie an easing to inflation rather than ease in response to say weak employment figures. So there is a good arguement to made that they may probably ease on Friday. Failing that, I would think the timing obviously is straight after the Reserve Bank board meeting in early August."
IAN BURNETT, HEAD FIXED INTEREST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:
"The figures were in line with our views. There was an initial rejection of new-highs in the market. The market is now fully priced for a 50 basis-point easing in monetary policy."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
